claims.claim: Microbial communities that develop in nectar through pollinator-mediated dispersal are often simple, dominated by one or a few species of nectar-specialist bacteria or yeast.
claims.source: Microbial communities that develop in nectar through this dispersal are often simple, dominated by one or a few species of nectar-specialist bacteria or yeast (Álvarez-Pérez et al., 2019; Golonka and Vilgalys, 2013; Herrera et al., 2010; Tsuji and Fukami, 2018; Warren et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on nectar microbial communities.

claims.claim: Hummingbird-mediated dispersal is highly stochastic because the pollinators differ in the species identity of yeasts and bacteria they carry on their beaks and tongues.
claims.source: Our previous work has shown that hummingbird-mediated dispersal is highly stochastic because the pollinators differ in the species identity of yeasts and bacteria they carry on their beaks and tongues (Morris et al., 2020; Toju et al., 2018; Vannette et al., 2021; Vannette and Fukami, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The outcome of local antagonistic interactions among microbial species can be sensitive to relative initial abundances.
claims.source: Additionally, the outcome of local antagonistic interactions among these microbial species can be sensitive to relative initial abundances (Dhami et al., 2016; Dhami et al., 2018; Grainger et al., 2019; Mittelbach et al., 2016; Peay et al., 2012; Tucker and Fukami, 2014; Vannette and Fukami, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature including the authors' own work.

claims.claim: Stochastic dispersal and history-dependent interactions jointly cause priority effects in nectar microbial communities.
claims.source: Together, the stochastic dispersal and the history-dependent interactions jointly cause priority effects in nectar microbial communities.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of previous findings cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Whether flowers are dominated by bacteria or yeasts can affect pollination and seed set.
claims.source: Moreover, recent studies indicate that whether flowers are dominated by bacteria or yeasts can affect pollination and seed set, although a mechanism for this effect remains unclear (de Vega et al., 2022; Good et al., 2014; Herrera et al., 2013; Jacquemyn et al., 2021; Junker et al., 2014; Rering et al., 2020; Schaeffer and Irwin, 2014; Vannette et al., 2013; Vannette and Fukami, 2016; Yang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: A total of 1152 flowers were sampled from 96 flowers at each of 12 sites along an approximately 200km coastline.
claims.source: Floral nectar was sampled from a total of 1152 flowers (96 flowers at each of 12 sites) along an approximately 200km coastline (Dhami et al., 2018; Tsuji et al., 2016; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology with data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Bacteria and yeasts were cultured on different media to characterize floral nectar communities.
claims.source: Bacteria and yeasts were cultured on different media to characterize floral nectar communities, which had been corroborated by molecular sequencing (Vannette and Fukami, 2017) and correlations between cell counts and colony forming units (Peay et al., 2012, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, validated by previous work.

claims.claim: D. aurantiacus flowers were frequently dominated by either bacteria or yeast, but rarely by both.
claims.source: Across all 12 sites, we found that D. aurantiacus flowers were frequently dominated by either bacteria or yeast, but rarely by both (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The observed proportions of co-dominated flowers were lower than expected by chance alone.
claims.source: This analysis showed that the observed proportions of co-dominated flowers were lower than expected by chance alone (Figure 2D; paired t-test: n=12, 95% CI [-5.3,–1.1], p=0.006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of field survey data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: There was no strong relationship between geographic distance and the difference in bacterial colonization between plant pairs.
claims.source: Contrary to this expectation, we found no strong relationship between distance and the difference in bacterial colonization (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, Figure 2—source data 2, LM: n=8775, p=0.07, R2=0.0003)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spatial data.

claims.claim: There was a slightly negative association between geographic distance and the difference in fungal colonization between plant pairs.
claims.source: and a slightly negative association between distance and the difference in fungal colonization (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, Figure 2—source data 2, LM: n=8775, p<0.05, R2=0.004), suggesting that spatial segregation is unlikely to explain the observed abundance pattern.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spatial data.

claims.claim: None of the climatic predictors (average annual temperature, temperature seasonality, annual precipitation, sampling date) were significant in predicting bacterial or yeast abundance.
claims.source: However, in a linear mixed model predicting bacterial or yeast abundance by average annual temperature, temperature seasonality, annual precipitation, sampling date, and site location included as a random effect, none of the predictors were significant (Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of environmental data.

claims.claim: M. reukaufii was the most frequently cultured species of fungi in D. aurantiacus nectar in the 12-site survey in 2015.
claims.source: Previously, we reported that M. reukaufii was the most frequently cultured species of fungi in D. aurantiacus nectar in the 12-site survey in 2015 (Table S2 in Dhami et al., 2018; see also Belisle et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Acinetobacter spp. were the dominant species of bacteria in D. aurantiacus nectar, followed by Neokomagataea sp.
claims.source: Namely, both culture-dependent and culture-independent methods indicate that Acinetobacter spp. were the dominant species of bacteria in D. aurantiacus nectar, followed by Neokomagataea (formerly Gluconobacter) sp. (see further detail in Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from multi-year surveys shown in Figure 3 and referenced in Appendix 1.

claims.claim: Species of Acinetobacter, Neokamagataea, Pseudomonas, and Metschnikowia have been shown to be common nectar specialists in other plants as well.
claims.source: The most common species of bacteria and yeast observed in our study system, such as species of Acinetobacter, Neokamagataea, Pseudomonas, and Metschnikowia, have been shown to be common nectar specialists in other plants as well (e.g., Fridman et al., 2012; Warren et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: A. nectaris and M. reukaufii would be a reasonable pair of species to focus on given their prevalence.
claims.source: Taken together, these independent pieces of information collectively indicate that, given their prevalence, A. nectaris and M. reukaufii would be a reasonable pair of species to focus on as a first step toward understanding the possible alternative states in the nectar microbial community of D. aurantiacus in our study landscape.
claims.evidence: This is a reasoning statement based on the integration of multiple lines of evidence.

claims.claim: A. nectaris exerted a strong inhibitory priority effect against M. reukaufii.
claims.source: We found that A. nectaris exerted a strong inhibitory priority effect against M. reukaufii (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 2)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: M. reukaufii exerted a priority effect against A. nectaris.
claims.source: We found that A. nectaris exerted a strong inhibitory priority effect against M. reukaufii (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 2) and vice versa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Higher densities of bacteria were tightly associated with lower nectar pH.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that higher densities of bacteria were tightly associated with lower nectar pH (Spearman rank-order: n=94, R2(adj.)=0.69, p=2.2 × 10–16, Figure 4B)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Higher densities of yeast were weakly associated with higher nectar pH.
claims.source: whereas higher densities of yeast were weakly associated with higher nectar pH (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Monoculture yeast grew poorly in low-pH nectar (pH = 3) when inoculated at low density.
claims.source: In addition, monoculture yeast grew poorly in low-pH nectar (pH = 3) when inoculated at low density (Figure 4C), but not if introduced at high density (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Bacterial growth was not affected by lowered nectar pH.
claims.source: Bacterial growth was not affected by lowered nectar pH (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: When yeast arrive first to nectar, they deplete nutrients such as amino acids and consequently limit bacterial growth, thereby avoiding pH-driven suppression.
claims.source: One likely reason for this density-dependent effect of pH on yeast is that, when yeast arrive first to nectar, they deplete nutrients such as amino acids and consequently limit bacterial growth, thereby avoiding pH-driven suppression that would happen if bacteria were initially abundant (Tucker and Fukami, 2014; Vannette and Fukami, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Larger yeast populations may have higher phenotypic heterogeneity, which increases the probability that the population will include cells that are resilient to low pH.
claims.source: Another possible reason is that larger yeast populations have higher phenotypic heterogeneity, which increases the probability that the population will include cells that are resilient to low pH. This mechanism has been suggested in the baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Guo and Olsson, 2016), although whether it applies to M. reukaufii remains to be tested.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on literature from a different yeast species.

claims.claim: The distribution of nectar pH in the field was non-unimodal.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that the distribution of nectar pH in the field was non-unimodal (Hartigan's dip test: n=576, D=0.05, p<2.2 × 10–16).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of field pH measurements.

claims.claim: A 3-mode model was a better fit than a 2-mode model for nectar pH distribution.
claims.source: Furthermore, a 3-mode model was a better fit than a 2-mode model (Likelihood ratio test: p=1.6 × 10–16, AICk=2 = 2365, AICk=3=2296, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical model comparison of field pH data.

claims.claim: Nectar pH had local modes at 7.8, 5.5, and 2.6 according to the mixture model.
claims.source: According to the mixture model we used, nectar pH had local modes at 7.8, 5.5, and 2.6 (Figure 5A, solid vertical lines)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical modeling of field pH data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The pH modes from field data (7.8, 5.5, 2.6) are strikingly similar to those from a previous laboratory experiment (Vannette et al., 2013).
claims.source: which are strikingly similar to those from the experiment we reported previously (Vannette et al., 2013), where filtered nectar from newly opened D. aurantiacus flowers was inoculated with no microbes, the yeast M. reukaufii, or the bacterium Neokomagataea sp. under controlled laboratory conditions (Figure 5A, dashed vertical lines).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between current field data and previous experimental data.

claims.claim: Older and pollinated flowers were more likely to have low nectar pH.
claims.source: In addition, we observed that older and pollinated flowers were more likely to have low nectar pH, reflecting the fact that, in these flowers, microbes would have more chance to grow and modify the nectar pH than in younger and non-pollinated flowers (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by field data shown in Figure 5B and supplementary figure.

claims.claim: The two sites (Jasper Ridge and San Gregorio) differed in their distributions of nectar pH.
claims.source: We also found that the two sites differed in their distributions of nectar pH (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by field data shown in Figure 5B and supplementary figure.

claims.claim: At Jasper Ridge, many of the pollinated flowers had low pH values consistent with bacterial dominance.
claims.source: At Jasper Ridge, many of the pollinated flowers had low pH values consistent with bacterial dominance.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from field data described in the text and shown in figures.

claims.claim: At San Gregorio, pollinated flowers had intermediate pH values that characterize yeast dominance.
claims.source: In contrast, at San Gregorio, these flowers had intermediate pH values that characterize yeast dominance.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from field data described in the text and shown in figures.

claims.claim: D. aurantiacus flowers with higher bacterial densities tended to have lower nectar pH at Stanford University's Dish hill.
claims.source: At another site within the region, Stanford University's Dish hill, we measured both nectar pH and bacterial growth and found that D. aurantiacus flowers with higher bacterial densities tended to have lower nectar pH (LMM: n=62, p=7.4 × 10–8) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of field data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Three genetically divergent strains of M. reukaufii were differentially affected by early arrival of A. nectaris.
claims.source: Through further laboratory experimentation, we also found that three genetically divergent strains of M. reukaufii, all of which were collected from the same site, Jasper Ridge, were differentially affected by early arrival of A. nectaris (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: One of the three yeast strains, MR1, was more negatively affected by priority effects than the other two strains, MY0182 and MY0202.
claims.source: Specifically, one of the three yeast strains, MR1, was more negatively affected by priority effects than the other two strains, MY0182 and MY0202, which were representative of distinct genotypic groups found across the 12 sites (Dhami et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work on genetic diversity.

claims.claim: Sites dominated by bacteria would be characterized by stronger selective pressure for yeasts to become more resistant to priority effects than sites dominated by yeasts.
claims.source: Given this genotypic and phenotypic variation among strains, it seemed conceivable that the site-to-site differences in the relative prevalence of yeasts and bacteria observed in the field could drive an eco-evolutionary feedback (sensu Post and Palkovacs, 2009), such that sites dominated by bacteria would be characterized by stronger selective pressure for yeasts to become more resistant to priority effects than sites dominated by yeasts (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observed variation and theoretical considerations.

claims.claim: Sixty days roughly corresponds to the duration of a typical flowering season of D. aurantiacus at Jasper Ridge.
claims.source: Sixty days roughly corresponds to the duration of a typical flowering season of D. aurantiacus at that site (Belisle et al., 2012) and some of the other sites we used for the field survey (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about the study system supported by citation.

claims.claim: Strain MR1 was chosen for experimental evolution because it was the most susceptible to priority effects.
claims.source: We chose strain MR1 for this experiment because it was the most susceptible to priority effects (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological decision based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Yeasts that evolved in low-pH and bacteria-conditioned nectars were less affected by priority effects than the ancestral yeast or the yeast evolved in the normal nectar.
claims.source: We found that, over the two months of serial transfers, yeasts that evolved in environments that constantly simulated early arrival of bacteria (bacteria-conditioned and low-pH nectars) were less affected by priority effects than the ancestral yeast or the yeast evolved in the normal nectar (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental evolution data shown in Figure 7A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The absolute growth of yeast evolved in bacteria-conditioned and low-pH nectars was less negatively affected by bacteria.
claims.source: This difference in the strength of priority effects reflects that the absolute growth of yeast evolved in bacteria-conditioned and low-pH nectars was less negatively affected by bacteria (Figure 7B, Figure 7—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The improved growth of evolved yeast was apparent only when bacteria were present.
claims.source: However, their improved growth was apparent only when bacteria were present (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Yeast can evolve to resist low pH over a duration that roughly corresponds to a single flowering season of D. aurantiacus.
claims.source: Together, these findings suggest that yeast can evolve to resist low pH, the very mechanism by which bacteria exert priority effects against yeast over a duration that roughly corresponds to a single flowering season of D. aurantiacus.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on experimental evolution results.

claims.claim: Strains that evolved stronger resistance to priority effects of pH-reducing bacteria became marginally worse at growing in neutral-pH monoculture.
claims.source: When considered across all experimental evolution treatments, strains that evolved stronger resistance to priority effects of pH-reducing bacteria became marginally worse at growing in neutral-pH monoculture (strains that are in the upper left quadrant in Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Strains that did not increase resistance to bacterial priority effects during experimental evolution were better able to grow in neutral-pH monoculture.
claims.source: Conversely, strains that did not increase resistance to bacterial priority effects during experimental evolution were better able to grow in neutral-pH monoculture (those in the upper right quadrant in monoculture) (LMM: n=48, p=0.05, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figure.

claims.claim: This type of evolutionary trade-off is the basis for the 'eco-evolutionary buffering' hypothesis recently proposed by Wittmann and Fukami, 2018.
claims.source: Incidentally, this type of evolutionary trade-off is the basis for the 'eco-evolutionary buffering' hypothesis recently proposed by Wittmann and Fukami, 2018.
claims.evidence: This is a connection to theoretical work cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Rapid evolution of resistance to priority effects under a trade-off constraint may partly explain why both yeast and bacteria persist in the field despite strong priority effects.
claims.source: Our finding here, that is rapid evolution of resistance to priority effects under a trade-off constraint, may partly explain why both yeast and bacteria persist in the field despite strong priority effects, but this possibility remains highly speculative at this stage.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: The ancestral strain exhibited heterozygosity at 25,820 sites across the 19 Mb diploid genome.
claims.source: We found that the ancestral strain exhibited heterozygosity at 25,820 sites across the 19 Mb diploid genome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome resequencing data.

claims.claim: Across all evolved lineages, there was an average of 142 sites exhibiting LOH per lineage (1699 total across all lineages).
claims.source: Across all evolved lineages, we observed an average of 142 sites exhibiting LOH per lineage (1699 total across all lineages).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis of evolved strains.

claims.claim: Most sites exhibiting LOH were shared across lineages and treatments (97%) and likely indicative of adaptation of this wild strain to the laboratory environment.
claims.source: Most sites exhibiting LOH were shared across lineages and treatments (97%) and likely indicative of adaptation of this wild strain to the laboratory environment.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of genomic data.

claims.claim: Several of the LOH events most predominant in the low-pH and bacteria-conditioned treatments fell near genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis.
claims.source: Several of the LOH events most predominant in the low-pH and bacteria-conditioned treatments fell near genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis (Figure 9—figure supplement 2, Figure 9—source data 2 for all treatments).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic annotation analysis shown in figures and source data.

claims.claim: Competition for amino acids has been suggested as a mechanism by which yeast species exert priority effects against bacteria and other species of yeast in this system.
claims.source: Competition for amino acids has been suggested as a mechanism by which yeast species exert priority effects against bacteria and other species of yeast in this system (Dhami et al., 2016; Peay et al., 2012; Tucker and Fukami, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Adaptation to limited amino acid availability could be associated with differential resistance to priority effects in low-pH environments.
claims.source: Our results suggest that adaptation to limited amino acid availability could be associated with differential resistance to priority effects in low-pH environments, though further experimentation is needed to determine the precise targets of selection.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of genomic data requiring further testing.

claims.claim: 146 putative de novo mutations were identified across all lineages, with an average of 12 putative de novo mutations per lineage.
claims.source: We identified 146 putative de novo mutations across all lineages, with an average of 12 putative de novo mutations per lineage (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The locations of putative de novo mutations displayed some spatial concordance with patterns of LOH.
claims.source: The locations of these mutations displayed some spatial concordance with patterns of LOH, corroborating the putative role of these genomic regions in adaptive evolution (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Yeast evolved in low-pH and bacteria-conditioned nectar both exhibited putative de novo mutations near genes involved in solute regulation.
claims.source: Yeast evolved in low-pH and bacteria-conditioned nectar both exhibited putative de novo mutations near genes involved in solute regulation, such as membrane transport, vesicle cargo recognition, and solute carrier proteins (Figure 9—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic annotation analysis.

claims.claim: Solute regulation has been implicated in adaptation to high-osmolarity environments.
claims.source: Solute regulation has been implicated in adaptation to high-osmolarity environments (Pozo et al., 2015), where osmotolerant yeast has been found to compete more strongly in sugar-rich nectar.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Strains evolved in low-pH nectar had repeated LOH events in genes associated with stress responses and growth, whereas strains evolved in bacteria-conditioned nectar did not.
claims.source: We also found some differences between yeast evolved in low-pH and bacteria-conditioned nectars. For example, strains evolved in low-pH nectar had repeated LOH events in genes associated with stress responses and growth, whereas strains evolved in bacteria-conditioned nectar did not.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis comparing different evolution treatments.

claims.claim: The observed patterns of phenotypic evolution were concurrent with changes in genomic variation.
claims.source: In summary, these results indicate that the observed patterns of phenotypic evolution were concurrent with changes in genomic variation.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis claim integrating phenotypic and genomic data.

claims.claim: Bacterial growth in nectar can negatively affect nectar consumption by pollinators, the probability of pollination, and the number of seeds produced by D. aurantiacus flowers.
claims.source: Prior work has shown that bacterial growth in nectar can negatively affect nectar consumption by pollinators, the probability of pollination, and the number of seeds produced by D. aurantiacus flowers (Vannette et al., 2013; Vannette and Fukami, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: For high amino acid nectar, less nectar was consumed from flowers with low-pH nectar.
claims.source: We found that for the high amino acid nectar, which resembled the synthetic nectar used in the previously described microcosm experiments, less nectar was consumed from flowers with low-pH nectar (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by field experimental data shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: Low pH, but not low concentrations of amino acids, was the primary factor that caused a reduction in nectar consumption.
claims.source: This result indicates that low pH, but not low concentrations of amino acids, was the primary factor that caused a reduction in nectar consumption.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the field experimental results.

claims.claim: Hummingbirds are less sensitive to the taste of amino acids.
claims.source: One possible explanation as to why hummingbirds responded less to amino acids than pH is that hummingbirds are less sensitive to the taste of amino acids (Baldwin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Bacteria-dominated flowers can negatively affect nectar consumption by pollinators by lowering nectar pH.
claims.source: Because the bacteria lower pH (Figures 4B and 5C), these findings suggest that bacteria-dominated flowers can negatively affect nectar consumption by pollinators by lowering nectar pH.
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting experimental results on pH effects to pollinator behavior.

claims.claim: Low nectar pH associated with bacteria-dominated flowers affects the relationship between plants and pollinators via microbial priority effects.
claims.source: Overall, these results, together with our previous findings (Vannette et al., 2013), suggest that in addition to impacting microbial interactions and community assembly, low nectar pH associated with bacteria-dominated flowers affects the relationship between plants and pollinators via microbial priority effects.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis claim integrating multiple lines of evidence.

claims.claim: pH is thought to be a strong predictor of community assembly in other microbial systems as well.
claims.source: pH is thought to be a strong predictor of community assembly in other microbial systems as well (Ratzke and Gore, 2018), including those in the soil (Fierer and Jackson, 2006; Tedersoo et al., 2014), the human gut (Beasley et al., 2015), and food products such as sourdough bread (Oshiro et al., 2020; Valmorri et al., 2008), cheese (Ferreira and Viljoen, 2003), and milk (Álvarez-Martín et al., 2008; Gadaga et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on various microbial systems.

claims.claim: Priority effects have been observed in some microbial habitats where pH is important.
claims.source: Priority effects have been observed in some of these microbial habitats, suggesting that pH may govern priority effects as an overarching factor across many types of microbial communities.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on the current study and literature.

claims.claim: pH-mediated priority effects give rise to bacterial and yeast dominance as alternative community states.
claims.source: Using nectar-inhabiting microbes, we have shown that pH-mediated priority effects (Figures 4 and 6) give rise to bacterial and yeast dominance as alternative community states (Figures 2, 3 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis claim integrating multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claims.claim: pH is not merely a mechanism of the priority effects, but it also determines the strength of the priority effects, fuels rapid evolution that changes the strength of the priority effects, and causes functional consequences of the priority effects for the host plants' reproduction.
claims.source: We have also shown, however, that pH is not merely a mechanism of the priority effects, but it also determines the strength of the priority effects, fuels rapid evolution that changes the strength of the priority effects (Figures 7—9), and causes functional consequences of the priority effects for the host plants' reproduction (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis claim integrating multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claims.claim: Historical contingency via priority effects can be understood more simply than generally thought once we identify a common factor that dictates various aspects of priority effects.
claims.source: These findings indicate that historical contingency via priority effects can be understood more simply than generally thought once we identify a common factor that dictates various aspects of priority effects.
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claims.claim: Field sampling was conducted at 12 sites throughout the San Francisco Peninsula.
claims.source: Field sampling was conducted at 12 sites throughout the San Francisco Peninsula (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology.

claims.claim: At each site, eight D. aurantiacus flowers with a closed stigma were harvested from 12 plants.
claims.source: At each site, eight D. aurantiacus flowers with a closed stigma were harvested from 12 plants.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology.

claims.claim: Flowers with a closed stigma are more likely to have been pollinated than flowers with an open stigma.
claims.source: Flowers with a closed stigma are more likely to have been pollinated than flowers with an open stigma (Fetscher and Kohn, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about the study organism supported by citation.

claims.claim: Molecular identification of colonies indicated that Neokomagataea sp. was capable of forming colonies on the chloramphenicol-supplemented YMA.
claims.source: Molecular identification of colonies via amplification and sequencing of ribosomal genes (16 S rDNA for bacteria and 28 S rDNA for fungi; Good et al., 2014) indicated that Neokomagataea sp. was capable of forming colonies on the chloramphenicol-supplemented YMA and that these bacterial colonies tended to be distinctly smaller than yeast colonies.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological observation from the study.

claims.claim: The dominant 45 taxa of bacteria and yeast recovered from culture-independent analyses also form colonies on R2A and YMA, respectively.
claims.source: In a previous study (Vannette and Fukami, 2014), Illumina MiSeq metabarcoding conducted on D. aurantiacus nectar samples indicated that the dominant 45 taxa of bacteria (e.g. Acinetobacter, Neokomagataea, and Pseudomonas spp.) and yeast (e.g. Metschnikowia, Starmerella, and Cryptococcus spp.) recovered from culture-independent analyses also form colonies on R2A and YMA, respectively (Aizenberg-Gershtein et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work validating culture methods.

claims.claim: Culture-based methods for estimating bacterial and yeast abundance should provide useful, though not perfectly precise, information on their abundances.
claims.source: Thus, our culture-based methods for estimating bacterial and yeast abundance should provide useful, though not perfectly precise, information on their abundances.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement acknowledging limitations.

claims.claim: The CLAM program was originally developed to classify species into habitat specialists and generalists.
claims.source: The CLAM program was originally developed to classify species into habitat specialists and generalists, focusing on two types of habitats, with species grouped into four categories: habitat A specialists, habitat B specialists, generalists, and species that are too rare to be classified into any of the other three groups.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a statistical method used in the study.

claims.claim: The same principle of CLAM can be applied to classifying microbial communities into bacteria-dominated, yeast-dominated, co-dominated, and microbial communities with too few bacteria and/or yeast for classification.
claims.source: The same principle can be applied to classifying microbial communities into bacteria-dominated, yeast-dominated, co-dominated, and microbial communities with too few bacteria and/or yeast for classification.

results.result: Field surveys of 1152 D. aurantiacus flowers across 12 sites revealed that flowers were frequently dominated by either bacteria or yeast, but rarely by both, with co-dominated flowers occurring less frequently than expected by chance. Nectar pH varied among flowers in a manner consistent with alternative stable states. Spatial segregation and climatic factors did not explain the observed abundance patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C23, and C24 are directly supported by field survey data (Figures 2, 5) and statistical analyses showing significantly fewer co-dominated flowers than expected (p=0.006). Claims C25-C27 provide additional support by ruling out spatial and climatic explanations through appropriate statistical tests. The sample size (n=1152) is substantial and the CLAM classification method is appropriately applied.

results.result: Multi-year surveys and molecular identification established that M. reukaufii was the most frequently cultured yeast species and Acinetobacter spp. were the dominant bacteria in D. aurantiacus nectar, making A. nectaris and M. reukaufii a reasonable focal pair for studying alternative states.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 are supported by multi-year survey data (Figure 3) and both culture-dependent and culture-independent methods. Claim C30 is supported by citations to previous literature. Claim C31 is a reasonable inference based on the prevalence data. The methodological validation through multiple approaches strengthens these findings.

results.result: Laboratory experiments demonstrated that A. nectaris exerted strong inhibitory priority effects against M. reukaufii (and vice versa) by reducing nectar pH. Higher bacterial densities were tightly associated with lower pH (R²=0.69, p=2.2×10⁻¹⁶), and monoculture yeast grew poorly in low-pH nectar when inoculated at low density, while bacterial growth was unaffected by pH.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C32-C37 are well-supported by experimental data (Figure 4) with appropriate statistical analyses and adequate sample sizes (n=94-128). The experiments manipulated arrival order and measured both pH and microbial growth, establishing a clear mechanistic link. The density-dependent effect of pH on yeast (C36) is demonstrated experimentally, though the mechanistic explanation remains partially speculative.

results.result: Field measurements of nectar pH showed a non-unimodal distribution best fit by a 3-mode model with modes at pH 7.8, 5.5, and 2.6, strikingly similar to previous laboratory experiments. Older and pollinated flowers had lower pH, and flowers with higher bacterial densities had lower pH (p=7.4×10⁻⁸).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C48 are supported by field pH measurements (n=576) with appropriate statistical tests (Hartigan's dip test, likelihood ratio test, linear mixed models). The tri-modal distribution and its correspondence to laboratory experiments (C43) provide strong evidence for pH-mediated alternative states. However, 21% of flowers had insufficient nectar for pH measurement, which could introduce bias if these flowers differ systematically.

results.result: Three genetically divergent strains of M. reukaufii from the same site were differentially affected by early arrival of A. nectaris, with strain MR1 being more negatively affected than strains MY0182 and MY0202.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by experimental data (Figure 6) showing strain-specific responses to bacterial priority effects. The statistical analysis appropriately accounts for experimental design with nested random effects. This variation among strains provides the foundation for the subsequent experimental evolution work.

results.result: Experimental evolution over 60 days (30 transfers) showed that M. reukaufii strain MR1 evolved increased resistance to bacterial priority effects when constantly exposed to low-pH or bacteria-conditioned nectar. The improved growth was apparent only when bacteria were present, suggesting evolution of pH resistance as the mechanism of bacterial priority effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C54-C57 are supported by experimental evolution data (Figure 7) with appropriate controls (ancestral and normal nectar treatments) and adequate replication (4 independent evolutionary replicates per treatment). The 60-day duration corresponds to a flowering season (C52), making the timescale ecologically relevant. Statistical analyses appropriately account for nested random effects and multiple rounds of experiments.

results.result: Strains that evolved stronger resistance to bacterial priority effects showed marginally worse growth in neutral-pH monoculture (p=0.05), suggesting an evolutionary trade-off. This trade-off may partly explain the persistence of both yeast and bacteria in the field despite strong priority effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by experimental data (Figure 8) but the statistical significance is marginal (p=0.05). Claim C59 provides supporting evidence for the trade-off. However, the authors themselves acknowledge that the explanation for field coexistence (C61) is 'highly speculative.' The trade-off is observed but its role in maintaining coexistence requires additional theoretical or empirical support.

results.result: Whole genome resequencing revealed that the ancestral strain had 25,820 heterozygous sites, with evolved lineages showing an average of 142 LOH events per lineage. Most LOH (97%) was shared across treatments, but treatment-specific LOH events in low-pH and bacteria-conditioned treatments fell near genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis, suggesting adaptation to limited amino acid availability may be associated with resistance to priority effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are well-supported by genomic data with adequate sequencing depth (444X). However, claims C65-C67 are more speculative. The association between LOH near amino acid biosynthesis genes and priority effect resistance is suggestive but not definitively established. The authors appropriately acknowledge that 'further experimentation is needed to determine the precise targets of selection' (C67). The limited statistical power (4 replicates per treatment) and lack of functional validation weaken these genomic interpretations.

results.result: 146 putative de novo mutations were identified across all lineages (average 12 per lineage), with spatial concordance to LOH patterns. Yeast evolved in low-pH and bacteria-conditioned nectar exhibited mutations near genes involved in solute regulation. Differences between treatments suggest multiple genomic strategies for resisting priority effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 are supported by genomic data, but the identification of de novo mutations relies on computational filtering that may not capture all true mutations or may include false positives. Claims C70-C72 identify candidate genes but lack functional validation. The connection to solute regulation (C71) is based on a single citation to a different system. Claim C73 is a reasonable synthesis but the genomic changes have not been causally linked to the observed phenotypic evolution.

results.result: Field experiments with artificial flowers showed that low nectar pH (pH=2) reduced nectar consumption by hummingbirds compared to neutral pH (pH=7) when amino acid concentrations were high. Low pH, rather than amino acid concentration, was the primary factor reducing consumption, suggesting bacteria-dominated flowers negatively affect pollination through pH reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C75-C76, and C78 are supported by field experimental data (Figure 10B) with adequate sample size (n=79 for the high amino acid treatment). The factorial design appropriately separates pH and amino acid effects. However, the effect was only observed in high amino acid nectar and not when sugar concentrations were altered (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), suggesting context-dependency. Claims C77 and C79 are reasonable inferences but C79 relies partly on previous work (Vannette et al., 2013) not fully presented here.

results.result: The study demonstrates that pH is an overarching factor governing multiple aspects of priority effects: it mediates the priority effects between bacteria and yeast, determines their strength, drives rapid evolution that changes priority effect strength, and causes functional consequences for plant reproduction. This shows that historical contingency via priority effects can be understood more simply than generally thought.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C82-C84 are synthesis claims integrating multiple lines of evidence from the study. The evidence for pH as a mechanism (C4, C32-C37), driver of alternative states (C2-C3, C40-C48), evolutionary force (C54-C57), and functional factor (C75-C76) is well-supported by the individual results. However, claim C84 makes a broad generalization about historical contingency that extends beyond this single system. The conclusion is well-supported for this system but the generalizability remains to be tested.

results.result: Two potential mechanisms explain the density-dependent effect of pH on yeast: (1) early-arriving yeast deplete amino acids, limiting bacterial growth and avoiding pH-driven suppression, and (2) larger yeast populations have higher phenotypic heterogeneity, increasing the probability of pH-resilient cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by citations to previous work (Tucker and Fukami, 2014; Vannette and Fukami, 2018) but not directly tested in this study. Claim C39 is explicitly speculative, based on work in S. cerevisiae, and the authors acknowledge it 'remains to be tested' in M. reukaufii. These are plausible hypotheses but lack direct experimental support in this manuscript.

results.result: Site-to-site differences in the relative prevalence of yeasts and bacteria could drive an eco-evolutionary feedback where bacteria-dominated sites exert stronger selective pressure for yeast resistance to priority effects than yeast-dominated sites.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is presented as a hypothesis ('it seemed conceivable') based on observed variation in strain susceptibility (C49-C50) and site-level differences (Figure 2B). While the components are supported (strain variation exists, sites differ in bacteria/yeast prevalence), the eco-evolutionary feedback itself is not directly tested. This would require showing that yeast strains from bacteria-dominated sites are more resistant to priority effects than strains from yeast-dominated sites, which is not demonstrated.

results.result: pH is a strong predictor of community assembly in other microbial systems (soil, human gut, food products), and priority effects have been observed in some of these habitats, suggesting pH may govern priority effects as an overarching factor across many types of microbial communities.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by citations to previous literature on various microbial systems. However, claim C81 is explicitly speculative ('suggesting that pH may govern'). The authors have demonstrated pH as an overarching factor in one system (nectar microbiome) but have not tested whether it plays the same role in other systems. This is a reasonable hypothesis for future work but not a supported conclusion from this study.
